claim: HnRNP A1 regulates many alternative splicing events by the recognition of splicing silencer elements.
source: HnRNP A1 regulates many alternative splicing events by the recognition of splicing silencer elements.
evidence: This is a general statement about hnRNP A1 function supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Both RRMs of hnRNP A1 can bind simultaneously to a single bipartite motif of the human intronic splicing silencer ISS-N1.
source: In addition, we show by NMR that both RRMs of hnRNP A1 can bind simultaneously to a single bipartite motif of the human intronic splicing silencer ISS-N1, which controls survival of motor neuron exon 7 splicing.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: RRM2 binds to the upstream motif and RRM1 to the downstream motif of ISS-N1.
source: RRM2 binds to the upstream motif and RRM1 to the downstream motif.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data and paramagnetic relaxation enhancement experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: The architecture and organization of the two RRMs is essential to hnRNP A1 function.
source: Combining the insights from the structure with in cell splicing assays we show that the architecture and organization of the two RRMs is essential to hnRNP A1 function.
evidence: This is supported by both structural data and functional splicing assays in cells.

claim: The disruption of the inter-RRM interaction impairs splicing repression by hnRNP A1.
source: The disruption of the inter-RRM interaction or the loss of RNA binding capacity of either RRM impairs splicing repression by hnRNP A1.
evidence: This is supported by splicing assays with interface mutants shown in Figure 5.

claim: The loss of RNA binding capacity of either RRM impairs splicing repression by hnRNP A1.
source: The disruption of the inter-RRM interaction or the loss of RNA binding capacity of either RRM impairs splicing repression by hnRNP A1.
evidence: This is supported by splicing assays with RRM mutants shown in Figure 5.

claim: Both binding sites within the ISS-N1 are important for splicing repression.
source: Furthermore, both binding sites within the ISS-N1 are important for splicing repression and their contributions are cumulative rather than synergistic.
evidence: This is supported by splicing assays with ISS-N1 mutants shown in Figure 5.

claim: The contributions of both binding sites within ISS-N1 are cumulative rather than synergistic.
source: Furthermore, both binding sites within the ISS-N1 are important for splicing repression and their contributions are cumulative rather than synergistic.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of splicing assays with single and double ISS-N1 mutants.

claim: HnRNP A1 participates in the processing of micro-RNA precursors.
source: For instance, hnRNP A1 participates in the processing of micro-RNA precursors (Guil and Cáceres, 2007; Michlewski et al., 2008; Choudhury and Michlewski, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: HnRNP A1 participates in the biogenesis and maintenance of telomeres.
source: in the biogenesis and maintenance of telomeres (LaBranche et al., 1998; Zhang et al., 2006; Flynn et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: HnRNP A1 participates in transcription regulation.
source: in transcription regulation (Fukuda et al., 2002; Campillos et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: HnRNP A1 participates in nucleo-cytoplasmic mRNA transport.
source: and in nucleo-cytoplasmic mRNA transport (Piñol-Roma and Dreyfuss, 1992; Izaurralde et al., 1997; Reed and Hurt, 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The best-characterized function of hnRNP A1 resides in its extensive implication in constitutive and alternative splicing.
source: However, the best-characterized function of hnRNP A1 resides in its extensive implication in constitutive and alternative splicing, where it generally acts as a splicing repressor in enhancing exon skipping (Mayeda and Krainer, 1992; Cáceres et al., 1994; Yang et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and represents established knowledge.

claim: HnRNP A1 generally acts as a splicing repressor in enhancing exon skipping.
source: However, the best-characterized function of hnRNP A1 resides in its extensive implication in constitutive and alternative splicing, where it generally acts as a splicing repressor in enhancing exon skipping (Mayeda and Krainer, 1992; Cáceres et al., 1994; Yang et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: HnRNP A1 plays a decisive role in the splicing regulation of exon 7 of the survival motor neuron (SMN) genes.
source: HnRNP A1 plays a decisive role in the splicing regulation of exon 7 of the survival motor neuron (SMN) genes.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the field.

claim: SMA originates from a deletion or a mutation within the SMN1 gene.
source: SMA originates from a deletion or a mutation within the SMN1 gene, which impairs the production of the SMN protein.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the genetic basis of SMA.

claim: A deletion or mutation within the SMN1 gene impairs the production of the SMN protein.
source: SMA originates from a deletion or a mutation within the SMN1 gene, which impairs the production of the SMN protein.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SMA pathology.

claim: The SMN2 gene is nearly identical to SMN1.
source: The SMN2 gene is nearly identical to SMN1 but fails to rescue the inactive SMN1 because a critical C-to-U change at position 6 of exon 7 strongly weakens exon 7 splicing (Lefebvre et al., 1995; Cartegni and Krainer, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SMN2 fails to rescue the inactive SMN1 because a critical C-to-U change at position 6 of exon 7 strongly weakens exon 7 splicing.
source: The SMN2 gene is nearly identical to SMN1 but fails to rescue the inactive SMN1 because a critical C-to-U change at position 6 of exon 7 strongly weakens exon 7 splicing (Lefebvre et al., 1995; Cartegni and Krainer, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The C-to-U change at position 6 of exon 7 transforms an exonic splicing enhancer (ESE) into an exonic splicing silencer (ESS).
source: This C-to-U change transforms an exonic splicing enhancer (ESE) into an exonic splicing silencer (ESS) (Cartegni and Krainer, 2002; Kashima and Manley, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: 80% of the transcripts originating from SMN2 lack exon 7.
source: As a consequence, the large majority (80%) of the transcripts originating from SMN2 lacks exon 7, resulting in an unstable protein product.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SMN2 splicing patterns.

claim: Transcripts from SMN2 lacking exon 7 result in an unstable protein product.
source: As a consequence, the large majority (80%) of the transcripts originating from SMN2 lacks exon 7, resulting in an unstable protein product.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SMN protein stability.

claim: The SMN2 gene produces 20% full-length transcripts and hence some functional SMN protein necessary for survival.
source: The gene still produces 20% full-length transcripts and hence some functional SMN protein necessary for survival (Lefebvre et al., 1995, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The SMN2 gene is a major modulator of the severity of SMA.
source: The SMN2 gene is a major modulator of the severity of SMA.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the SMA field.

claim: Increasing the amount of functional SMN protein by restoring an SMN1-like splicing pattern in SMN2 is a very promising approach for SMA treatments.
source: Increasing the amount of functional SMN protein by restoring an SMN1-like splicing pattern in SMN2 is a very promising approach for SMA treatments (Foust et al., 2010; Hua et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Anti-sense oligonucleotides (ASO) targeting ISS-N1 enhance SMN2 exon 7 inclusion in cell culture.
source: Anti-sense oligonucleotides (ASO) targeting a strong intronic splicing silencer (ISS) at the beginning of intron 7 (named ISS-N1), which contains a bipartite motif bound by hnRNP A1, have been shown to enhance SMN2 exon 7 inclusion in cell culture (Hua et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Anti-sense oligonucleotides (ASO) targeting ISS-N1 enhance SMN2 exon 7 inclusion in SMA mouse models.
source: and in SMA mouse models (Hua et al., 2011, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The ASO targeting ISS-N1 has successfully passed a clinical research program for the treatment of children with SMA.
source: This ASO has successfully passed a clinical research program for the treatment of children with SMA (Chiriboga et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a clinical study.

claim: The ASO targeting ISS-N1 has been approved by the FDA for treatment of SMA licensed under the name SPINRAZA (Nusinersen).
source: and has recently been approved by the FDA for treatment of SMA licensed under the name SPINRAZA (Nusinersen).
evidence: This is a factual statement about FDA approval.

claim: The N-terminal part of hnRNP A1 (UP1) contains two closely related RNA recognition motifs (RRM1 and RRM2) responsible for the specific RNA-binding properties.
source: This is achieved by the N-terminal part of the protein, also referred to as unwinding protein 1 (UP1), which contains two closely related RNA recognition motifs (RRM1 and RRM2) responsible for the specific RNA-binding properties (Burd and Dreyfuss, 1994; Maris et al., 2005).

claim: The RRMs of hnRNP A1 are followed by a glycine-rich C-terminal region (G-domain) with both protein- and RNA-binding properties.
source: The RRMs are followed by a glycine-rich C-terminal region (G-domain) with both protein- and RNA-binding properties (Kumar et al., 1990; Cartegni et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The G-domain is not essential for RNA binding.
source: While not essential for RNA binding, the G-domain has been shown to be critical for correct splice site selection (Blanchette and Chabot, 1999)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The G-domain has been shown to be critical for correct splice site selection.
source: While not essential for RNA binding, the G-domain has been shown to be critical for correct splice site selection (Blanchette and Chabot, 1999)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The G-domain is involved in liquid droplet formation.
source: and to be involved in liquid droplet formation (Lin et al., 2015; Molliex et al., 2015).

claim: The G-domain is required for cooperative RNA binding.

claim: Cooperative RNA binding by hnRNP A1 can be directional in the 3´−5´direction and extend over tens of bases.
source: Moreover, it is required for cooperative RNA binding (Zhu et al., 2001) that can be directional in the 3´−5´direction and extend over tens of bases (Okunola and Krainer, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The two RRMs of hnRNP A1 are neither redundant nor functionally equivalent.
source: Although the two RRMs are highly alike (35% identical and 60% similar), they are neither redundant nor functionally equivalent.

source: Indeed, chimeric proteins constructed by duplication, swapping or deletion of the RRMs affect hnRNP A1 alternative splicing properties differently (Mayeda et al., 1998).

claim: HnRNP A1 RRMs interact with one another and adopt a single defined orientation.

claim: RRMs are asymmetric binding platforms.
source: Since RRMs are asymmetric binding platforms (Maris et al., 2005), the mode of RNA binding is strongly restricted by the relative orientation of the RRMs (reviewed in [Barraud and Allain, 2013]).

claim: The mode of RNA binding is strongly restricted by the relative orientation of the RRMs.
source: Since RRMs are asymmetric binding platforms (Maris et al., 2005), the mode of RNA binding is strongly restricted by the relative orientation of the RRMs (reviewed in [Barraud and Allain, 2013]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review.

claim: The NMR signals from the β1-α1 loop region in RRM2 are absent from both the free and bound spectra, reflecting a conformational dynamic for this loop.
source: The NMR signals from the corresponding region in RRM2 (β1-α1 loop) are absent from both the free and bound spectra, reflecting a conformational dynamic for this loop.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data.

claim: Intermolecular contacts between the β1-α1 loop region and U1 cannot be observed in solution for RRM2.
source: As a consequence, intermolecular contacts between this region and U1 cannot be observed in solution, although intermolecular contacts were seen to the equivalent of U1 in the structure of UP1-DNA (Ding et al., 1999).
evidence: This is inference from the absence of NMR signals and comparison to a previous structure.

claim: The nucleotides at the 3´-end, U5 and U6, are not interacting with RRM2 and are highly disordered in the structural ensemble.
source: The nucleotides at the 3´-end, U5 and U6 are not interacting with RRM2 and are therefore highly disordered in the structural ensemble.
evidence: This is supported by the NMR structure.

claim: The side chain of Arg140 is potentially interacting with the phosphate group bridging G4 and U5 in the RRM2 complex.
source: Finally, the side chain of Arg140 is potentially interacting with the phosphate group bridging G4 and U5 (Figure 2B), since this contact is observed in eight conformers of the ensemble.
evidence: This is supported by the NMR structure ensemble.

claim: The optimal RNA-binding motif for RRM1 is 5´-YAGG-3´.
source: Combining our NMR study with the known structural and biochemical information on hnRNP A1 RNA-binding (Burd and Dreyfuss, 1994; Abdul-Manan and Williams, 1996; Ding et al., 1999; Myers and Shamoo, 2004; Bruun et al., 2016), we can decipher that the optimal RNA-binding motifs should be: 5´-YAGG-3´ and 5´-YAGN-3´ for RRM1 and RRM2, respectively, where Y is a pyrimidine and N any nucleotide.
evidence: This is inference from structural data and comparison to previous studies.

claim: The optimal RNA-binding motif for RRM2 is 5´-YAGN-3´.
source: Combining our NMR study with the known structural and biochemical information on hnRNP A1 RNA-binding (Burd and Dreyfuss, 1994; Abdul-Manan and Williams, 1996; Ding et al., 1999; Myers and Shamoo, 2004; Bruun et al., 2016), we can decipher that the optimal RNA-binding motifs should be: 5´-YAGG-3´ and 5´-YAGN-3´ for RRM1 and RRM2, respectively, where Y is a pyrimidine and N any nucleotide.
evidence: This is inference from structural data and comparison to previous studies.

claim: Mutating Arg55 to alanine lowers the affinity of RRM1 for RNA drastically by more than 50-fold.
source: In perfect agreement with the structure of the RRM1-RNA complex, mutating Arg55 to alanine lowers the affinity for the RNA drastically by more than 50-fold (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Table 2.

claim: Mutation of Arg92 resulted in an affinity decrease by 10-fold for RRM1.
source: Mutation of Arg92 or Asp42 also resulted in an affinity decrease by 10- and 3-fold, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Table 2.

claim: Mutation of Asp42 resulted in an affinity decrease by 3-fold for RRM1.
source: Mutation of Arg92 or Asp42 also resulted in an affinity decrease by 10- and 3-fold, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Table 2.

claim: RRM1 has a preference for a guanosine 3´ to the AG core.
source: This confirmed the RRM1 preference for a guanosine 3´ to the AG core (Figure 1F and Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by structural data and ITC measurements.

claim: Phe23 does not contribute significantly to RNA binding for RRM1 in terms of detectable affinity.
source: Removal of the side-chain (Table 2) as well as shortening or elongating the RNA at the 5´ end (Table 3), showed that Phe23 does not contribute significantly to RNA binding for these sequences, at least in terms of detectable affinity.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Tables 2 and 3.

claim: Mutating Arg140 led to a two-fold lower affinity for RRM2, underlining its importance for RNA binding.
source: Similarly for RRM2, removing contacts to the phosphate backbone by mutating Arg140 led to a two-fold lower affinity underlining its importance for RNA binding (Figure 2B and Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Table 2.

claim: Mutation of Met186 resulted in a 3-fold affinity drop for RRM2, confirming the contribution of helix α3 for RNA binding.
source: Also, confirming the contribution of helix α3 for RNA binding, mutation of Met186 resulted in a 3-fold affinity drop (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Table 2 and NMR data in the figure supplement.

claim: Removal of the hydroxyl group of Tyr167 (Y167F) has no effect on RNA binding by RRM2.
source: A role for Tyr167 in recognizing C2 could not be confirmed by ITC, since removal of the hydroxyl group (Y167F) has no effect on RNA binding (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Table 2.

claim: RRM2 can accommodate a C at the position preceding the AG core by having Glu176 stack under the base.
source: Our structure helps in understanding how RRM2 can accommodate a C at the position preceding the AG core. While a U is specifically recognized by Glu176 via a direct hydrogen-bond to the base (Ding et al., 1999; Myers and Shamoo, 2004), when a C is present Glu176 stacks under the base (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by the NMR structure and comparison to previous structures.

claim: RRM2 prefers a U at the position preceding the AG core.
source: Note that as for RRM1, RRM2 prefers a U at this position (see Table 3)
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Table 3.

claim: Both RRMs of hnRNP A1 have a preference for the 5´-UAGG-3´ motif.
source: First, both RRMs have a preference for the 5´-UAGG-3´ motif, which was indeed present in many RNAs found by SELEX or iCLIP (Burd and Dreyfuss, 1994; Bruun et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by ITC measurements and comparison to previous studies.

claim: Both RRMs of hnRNP A1 are tolerant to accommodate a cytosine 5´ to the AG core, extending the recognition motif to 5´-U/CAGG-3´.
source: Second, both RRMs are tolerant to accommodate a cytosine 5´ to the AG core, extending the recognition motif to 5´-U/CAGG-3´.
evidence: This is supported by ITC measurements and structural data.

claim: RRM2 is less affected by the replacement of the guanosine 3´ of the AG core than RRM1.
source: Finally, RRM2 is less affected by the replacement of the guanosine 3´ of the AG core than RRM1.
evidence: This is supported by ITC measurements shown in Table 3.

claim: The optimal recognition motif for RRM1 is 5´-U/CAGG-3´.
source: Overall, the optimal recognition motif for RRM1 can be finalized as 5´-U/CAGG-3´ and for RRM2 as 5´-U/CAGN-3´.
evidence: This is inference from ITC and structural data.

claim: The optimal recognition motif for RRM2 is 5´-U/CAGN-3´.
source: Overall, the optimal recognition motif for RRM1 can be finalized as 5´-U/CAGG-3´ and for RRM2 as 5´-U/CAGN-3´.
evidence: This is inference from ITC and structural data.

claim: RRM2 consistently has a higher affinity than RRM1 for all ITC measurements with isolated RRMs.
source: Importantly, for all these ITC measurements, RRM2 appears to consistently have a higher affinity than RRM1.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Tables 2 and 3.

claim: The inter-RRM linker (IRL) may be equivalent to RRM2 helix α3.
source: However, the available structures of UP1 (Ding et al., 1999; Myers and Shamoo, 2004; Morgan et al., 2015) suggest that the inter-RRM linker (IRL), which is missing from our RRM1 construct, may be equivalent to RRM2 helix α3.
evidence: This is inference from comparison to previous structures.

claim: In the context of UP1, both RRMs have very similar affinities for all tested RNA sequences.
source: In this context, both RRMs have now very similar affinities for all the tested sequences.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Table 4.

claim: The affinity of RRM1 for all oligonucleotides was significantly increased (over 5-fold) in the context of UP1 compared to isolated RRM1.
source: The affinity of RRM1 for all oligonucleotides was significantly increased (over 5-fold) while RRM2 kept the same affinity for RNA in both contexts (Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Table 4.

claim: RRM2 kept the same affinity for RNA in both isolated and UP1 contexts.
source: The affinity of RRM1 for all oligonucleotides was significantly increased (over 5-fold) while RRM2 kept the same affinity for RNA in both contexts (Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Table 4.

claim: The mutations in UP1-R1r2 and UP1-r1R2 were efficient in removing the RNA binding ability of the mutated RRM.
source: Importantly, the mutations were efficient in removing the RNA binding ability of the mutated RRM.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data showing N-values of ~1.

claim: The N-values of ITC measurements were robustly ~1, indicative of a 1:1 stoichiometry of the complex.
source: After fitting with a 1:1 binding model the obtained N-values of our ITC measurements were robustly ~1. This is indicative of a 1:1 stoichiometry of the complex.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data.

claim: RRM1 in the context of UP1 appears less affected by the replacement of the G following the AG core (~2 fold drop in affinity) than in the isolated RRM1 construct (at least 10-fold drop in affinity).
source: Intriguingly, RRM1 in the context of UP1 appears less affected by the replacement of the G following the AG core (~2 fold drop in affinity; Table 4) than in the isolated RRM1 construct (at least 10-fold drop in affinity; Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Table 4.

claim: Both RRMs of hnRNP A1 interact with ISS-N1.
source: Although both RRMs are seen to interact with ISS-N1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), some signals at the binding interface disappeared upon RNA addition.
evidence: This is supported by NMR titration data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: The complex between UP1 and ISS-N1 is in intermediate exchange.
source: This is indicative of a complex in intermediate exchange for which structure determination is difficult to achieve (Dominguez et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inference from NMR data and citation to a methodological reference.

claim: Introducing guanines downstream of the AG core dinucleotide increases the affinity of hnRNP A1 for ISS-N1.
source: Briefly, we introduced guanines downstream of the AG core dinucleotide to increase the affinity (Table 4), creating the RNA mutants ISS-N1-c14g, ISS-N1-u25g, and ISS-N1-14g25g (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on previous ITC data showing preference for guanine at this position.

claim: Combining the protein mutant UP1-R140A with RNA mutants gave NMR spectra of much improved quality.
source: Combining this protein mutant with the previous RNA mutants gave NMR spectra of much improved quality (Figure 3A–D), especially for the double mutant ISS-N1-14g25g and the single mutant ISS-N1-u25g.
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectra shown in Figure 3.

claim: RRM1 binds to the 3´-motif of ISS-N1 irrespective of the point mutations introduced in the RNA.
source: In addition, a detailed analysis of these NMR titrations (Figure 3E–H) strongly suggested that RRM1 binds to the 3´-motif of ISS-N1 irrespective of the point mutations introduced in the RNA and therefore RRM2 binds the 5´-motif (See Appendix 2 for details).
evidence: This is supported by detailed NMR analysis shown in Figure 3 and Appendix 2.

claim: The pattern of chemical shift changes observed for UP1 binding to one equivalent of ISS-N1 is highly similar to those observed for the individual RRMs bound to short RNA oligonucleotides.
source: Importantly, the pattern of chemical shift changes observed for UP1 binding to one equivalent of ISS-N1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) is highly similar to those observed for the individual RRMs bound to short RNA oligonucleotides (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of NMR data shown in the figure supplements.

claim: Only one molecule of hnRNP A1 binds ISS-N1.
source: This shows that only one molecule of hnRNP A1 binds and confirms the involvement of both RRMs of hnRNP A1 in ISS-N1 binding.
evidence: This is inference from NMR chemical shift data.

claim: The binding mode of UP1 to ISS-N1 resembles the one determined for RRMs in isolation.
source: The binding mode resembles the one determined for RRMs in isolation (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This is inference from comparison of NMR data.

claim: 87 unambiguous intermolecular protein-RNA contacts were observed with the assigned nucleotides in the UP1-R140A:ISS-N1-u25g complex.
source: Overall we observed 87 unambiguous intermolecular protein-RNA contacts with the assigned nucleotides (Appendix 2—table 2, Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in the appendix and figure supplements.

claim: The network of intermolecular contacts clearly supports the topology of RNA binding suggested by the NMR titrations.
source: Nevertheless, the obtained network of intermolecular contacts clearly supports the topology of RNA binding suggested by the NMR titrations.
evidence: This is inference from NMR data.

claim: Residues from RRM1 display many intermolecular contacts to the 3´-end of ISS-N1, namely to A22A23G24G25.
source: Indeed, the residues from RRM1 display many intermolecular contacts to the 3´-end of ISS-N1, namely to A22A23G24G25 and residues from RRM2 to the 5´-end, namely C11A12G13 (Appendix 2—table 2).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in the appendix.

claim: Residues from RRM2 display intermolecular contacts to the 5´-end of ISS-N1, namely C11A12G13.
source: Indeed, the residues from RRM1 display many intermolecular contacts to the 3´-end of ISS-N1, namely to A22A23G24G25 and residues from RRM2 to the 5´-end, namely C11A12G13 (Appendix 2—table 2).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in the appendix.

claim: PRE data shows that the spin-label attached near the 3´-end of ISS-N1 affects signals mostly from RRM1 and the interdomain linker.
source: Comparison of the spectra of the oxidized vs. reduced spin label shows that the signals affected by the presence of the paramagnetic probe originated mostly from RRM1 and the interdomain linker matching perfectly our previous experimental data.
evidence: This is supported by PRE data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The local perturbation in RRM1 and the interdomain linker by the spin-label is observed for both UP1 constructs (wild-type and R140A).
source: We observe this local perturbation in RRM1 and the interdomain linker for both UP1 constructs (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is supported by PRE data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The PRE data constitutes independent evidence that UP1 binds to the ISS-N1 using both RRMs, with RRM1 binding to the 3´ AG-motif and RRM2 to the 5´ AG-motif.
source: Altogether, this constitutes an independent evidence that UP1 binds to the ISS-N1 using both RRMs, and that RRM1 binds to the 3´ AG-motif and RRM2 to the 5´ AG-motif, as schematically represented on Figure 4E.
evidence: This is inference from PRE data shown in Figure 4.

claim: These results represent the first clear demonstration that two RRMs of the same hnRNP A1 molecule can bind the same RNA molecule simultaneously.
source: To our knowledge, these results represent the first clear demonstration that two RRMs of the same hnRNP A1 molecule can bind the same RNA molecule simultaneously.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: The structural model of UP1 bound to ISS-N1 differs strongly from the crystal structure of hnRNP A1 RRMs bound to telomeric DNA repeats.
source: Our structural model (Figure 4F) differs strongly from the crystal structure of hnRNP A1 RRMs bound to telomeric DNA repeats, where hnRNP A1 dimerizes and binds to two distinct DNA oligonucleotides (Appendix 1—figure 1), and where RRM1 binds the 5´-end of a DNA molecule and RRM2 the 3´-end of another DNA strand (Ding et al., 1999).
evidence: This is comparison of the current structural model to a previous structure.

claim: The antiparallel organization of hnRNP A1 RRM1 and RRM2 imposes a looping of the RNA molecule.
source: With our structural model, the antiparallel organization of hnRNP A1 RRM1 and RRM2 imposes a looping of the RNA molecule, such as suggested for other hnRNP family members with interacting RRMs adopting a single defined orientation (reviewed in [Barraud and Allain, 2013]).
evidence: This is inference from the structural model and comparison to other hnRNP family members.

claim: To adopt the mode of binding observed in the structural model, the RNA spacer between the 3´- and 5´-motifs must be sufficiently long.
source: To adopt this mode of binding, the RNA spacer between the 3´- and 5´-motifs must be sufficiently long.
evidence: This is inference from the structural model.

claim: The RNA spacer between the two AG motifs in ISS-N1 is 9-nucleotide long.
source: In the case of the ISS-N1, the RNA spacer between the two AG motifs is 9-nucleotide long (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the ISS-N1 sequence.

claim: Due to topological constraints, the RNA spacer between the two AGs must be at least 4-nucleotide long.
source: With various calculations of structural models where we reduced the length of the RNA spacer, we could see that due to topological constraints, the RNA spacer between the two AGs must be at least 4-nucleotide long (see Appendix 2 for details).
evidence: This is inference from structural modeling calculations.

claim: The ISS-N1 has regulatory function for SMN2 splicing.
source: Previous research has underlined the importance and regulatory function of the ISS-N1 for SMN2 splicing (Singh et al., 2006; Hua et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The two RRMs of hnRNP A1 have distinct roles in alternative splicing.
source: and while it has been shown that the two RRMs of hnRNP A1 have distinct roles in alternative splicing (Mayeda et al., 1998), our structural work does not prove that the two RRMs effectively bind the bipartite ISS-N1 in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: For RRM1 to bind with high affinity, the IRL must be positioned such as to sandwich the RNA together with the β-sheet surface of RRM1.
source: For RRM1 to bind with high affinity, the IRL must be positioned such as to sandwich the RNA together with the β-sheet surface of RRM1.
evidence: This is inference from structural data.

claim: The proper positioning of the IRL is achieved by RRM2 contacting RRM1 through a network of interactions including two salt bridges (Arg88-Asp157 and Arg75-Asp155).
source: This proper positioning of the IRL is achieved by RRM2 contacting RRM1 through a network of interactions including two salt bridges (Arg88-Asp157 and Arg75-Asp155)(Ding et al., 1999; Barraud and Allain, 2013; Morgan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Any disruption of the inter-RRM interaction should impair hnRNP A1 splicing regulation if the inter-RRM orientation is linked to the function.
source: If the inter-RRM orientation is linked to the function, any disruption of this interaction should impair hnRNP A1 splicing regulation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to be tested.

claim: The mutations in hnRNP A1 INT1, INT2, and INT3 interfere with the RRMs' interactions.
source: Using NMR, we could show that the mutations interfere with the RRMs' interactions.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The determined correlation time τc suggests a significant disruption of the inter-RRM interface by the mutations.
source: The determined correlation time τc suggests a significant disruption of the interface (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), which is also reflected by the chemical shift changes observed at the RRM interfaces for the mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mutations do not render the RRMs fully independent, possibly due to a strong topological constraint imposed by the IRL.
source: Nevertheless, the mutations do not render the RRMs fully independent (the changes in τc are modest), possibly due to a strong topological constraint imposed by the IRL.
evidence: This is inference from NMR data with speculation about the cause.

claim: Overexpression of hnRNP A1 can lower SMN1 exon 7 inclusion down to 6%.
source: We chose the SMN1 minigene system (Lefebvre et al., 1995; Frugier et al., 2002), where exon 7 inclusion occurs by default at 93% (Figure 5A, lane 1) and overexpression of hnRNP A1 can lower exon 7 inclusion down to 6% (Figure 5A, lane 2).
evidence: This is supported by splicing assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The three interface mutants INT1-3 consistently had a significant impact on SMN1 exon 7 splicing.
source: Our three interface mutants INT1-3 consistently had a significant impact on SMN1 exon 7 splicing (Figure 5A, lane 3–5).
evidence: This is supported by splicing assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The interface mutants lowered exon 7 inclusion down to 25–43%, but were not capable of repressing splicing to the same extent as the wild-type protein.
source: The interface mutants lowered exon 7 inclusion down to 25–43%, but were not capable of repressing splicing to the same extent as the wild-type protein, indicating that the relative orientation of the hnRNP A1 RRMs is essential for an optimal functioning in splicing repression.
evidence: This is supported by splicing assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The relative orientation of the hnRNP A1 RRMs is essential for an optimal functioning in splicing repression.
source: The interface mutants lowered exon 7 inclusion down to 25–43%, but were not capable of repressing splicing to the same extent as the wild-type protein, indicating that the relative orientation of the hnRNP A1 RRMs is essential for an optimal functioning in splicing repression.
evidence: This is inference from splicing assay data.

claim: Having only one functional RRM for RNA binding significantly impairs exon 7 splicing repression by hnRNP A1 for both RRM2 (R1r2) and RRM1 (r1R2).
source: Having only one functional RRM for RNA binding significantly impairs exon 7 splicing repression by hnRNP A1 for both RRM2 (R1r2) and RRM1 (r1R2) (90% and 83% exon 7 inclusion, respectively) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by splicing assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Binding of both RRMs of hnRNP A1 to RNA is required for achieving optimal repression of exon 7 inclusion.
source: This establishes that binding of both RRMs of hnRNP A1 to RNA is required for achieving optimal repression of exon 7 inclusion.
evidence: This is inference from splicing assay data.

claim: In the absence of hnRNP A1 overexpression, 36% exon 7 inclusion is observed for SMN2 WT.
source: In the absence of hnRNP A1 overexpression, we can observe 36% exon 7 inclusion for SMN2 WT, which can be significantly lowered to 24% upon hnRNP A1 overexpression (Figure 5C,E).
evidence: This is supported by splicing assay data shown in Figure 5C,E.

claim: HnRNP A1 overexpression can significantly lower SMN2 exon 7 inclusion to 24%.
source: In the absence of hnRNP A1 overexpression, we can observe 36% exon 7 inclusion for SMN2 WT, which can be significantly lowered to 24% upon hnRNP A1 overexpression (Figure 5C,E).
evidence: This is supported by splicing assay data shown in Figure 5C,E.

claim: Removal of the RNA-binding ability of a single RRM impairs splicing repression (R1r2 49%, r1R2 40%).
source: Removal of the RNA-binding ability of a single RRM impairs splicing repression (R1r2 49%, r1R2 40%, Figure 5C,E).
evidence: This is supported by splicing assay data shown in Figure 5C,E.

claim: The hnRNP A1 R1r2 mutant results in higher exon 7 inclusion than no hnRNP A1 overexpression in the SMN2 system.
source: However, while r1R2 has a tendency to have no impact on exon 7 inclusion compared to no hnRNP A1 overexpression, the R1r2 mutant results in an even higher exon 7 inclusion.
evidence: This is supported by splicing assay data shown in Figure 5C,E.

claim: The dominant negative effect observed for the RRM2 mutant in the context of SMN2 splicing suggests that the RRMs are non-equivalent.
source: Additionally, the dominant negative effect observed for the RRM2 mutant in the context of SMN2 splicing suggests that the RRMs are non-equivalent and that both RRMs of hnRNP A1 are required for SMN exon 7 splicing repression.
evidence: This is inference from splicing assay data.

claim: Both RRMs of hnRNP A1 are required for SMN exon 7 splicing repression.
source: Additionally, the dominant negative effect observed for the RRM2 mutant in the context of SMN2 splicing suggests that the RRMs are non-equivalent and that both RRMs of hnRNP A1 are required for SMN exon 7 splicing repression.
evidence: This is inference from splicing assay data.

claim: Co-transfection of hnRNP A1 R1r2 and hnRNP A1 r1R2 could not rescue splicing.
source: In support of our model, we could not observe any rescue of hnRNP A1 function when co-transfecting with the two RRM mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by splicing assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Mutation of both AG core dinucleotides to AA (ISS-N1-13a24a) raises SMN2 exon 7 inclusion to 61%.
source: Mutation of both AG core dinucleotides to AA (ISS-N1-13a24a) raises as expected SMN2 exon 7 inclusion to 61%.
evidence: This is supported by splicing assay data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: Overexpression of hnRNP A1 can reduce the level of exon 7 inclusion to 45% for ISS-N1-13a24a but not to the same level as in the wild-type SMN2-minigene (24%).
source: Overexpression of hnRNP A1 can still reduce the level of exon 7 inclusion (45%) but not to the same level as in the wild-type SMN2-minigene (24%).
evidence: This is supported by splicing assay data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: Removal of either the upstream or downstream AG (ISS-N1-g13a, ISS-N1-g24a) increases exon 7 inclusion to 48% and 46%, respectively.
source: Removal of either the upstream or downstream AG (ISS-N1-g13a, ISS-N1-g24a) also increases exon 7 inclusion to 48% and 46%, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by splicing assay data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: HnRNP A1 overexpression can partially suppress exon 7 inclusion to 32% and 30% for ISS-N1-g13a and ISS-N1-g24a, respectively.
source: This can be partially suppressed to 32% and 30%, respectively, by hnRNP A1 overexpression for both ISS-N1 mutants (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is supported by splicing assay data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: The effect observed for the ISS-N1-13a24a mutant is approximately the sum of the effects of the two single-substitutions, suggesting an additive rather than a synergistic effect of the two motifs for splicing repression.
source: The effect observed for the ISS-N1-13a24a mutant is approximately the sum of the effects of the two single-substitutions, suggesting an additive rather than a synergistic effect of the two motifs for splicing repression.
evidence: This is inference from quantitative analysis of splicing assay data.

claim: Both RNA-binding sites of the ISS-N1 are equally important for splicing repression of exon 7.
source: Altogether, this shows that both RNA-binding sites of the ISS-N1 are equally important for splicing repression of exon 7.
evidence: This is inference from splicing assay data with ISS-N1 mutants.

claim: Transfection of the SMN2 minigene containing ISS-N1 −6 and ISS-N1 −8 showed a significant increase in exon 7 inclusion.
source: Transfection of the SMN2 minigene containing the 2-nt deletions showed a significant increase in exon 7 inclusion for ISS-N1 −6 and ISS-N1 −8.
evidence: This is supported by splicing assay data shown in Figure 5F,G.

claim: The ISS-N1 −2 and ISS-N1 −4 SMN2 minigene mutants showed no aberration of the splicing pattern in the absence of hnRNP A1 overexpression.
source: In contrast the ISS-N1 −2 and ISS-N1 −4 SMN2 minigene mutants showed no aberration of the splicing pattern (Figure 5F,G), although this is only observed in the absence of any overexpression of hnRNP A1.
evidence: This is supported by splicing assay data shown in Figure 5F,G.

claim: Splicing repression by hnRNP A1 via the ISS-N1 tends to be less effective when the spacer spans less than four nucleotides.
source: In support of our model, splicing repression by hnRNP A1 via the ISS-N1 tends to be less effective when the spacer spans less than four nucleotides.
evidence: This is inference from splicing assay data with spacer length variants.

claim: A single hnRNP A1 molecule recognizes both AG-motifs of ISS-N1 using both RRMs (RRM2 binding upstream and RRM1 binding downstream) in a context where both RRMs interact intramolecularly.
source: Altogether, our splicing functional data in cells are in perfect agreement with the proposal that a single hnRNP A1 molecule recognizes both AG-motifs of ISS-N1 using both RRMs (RRM2 binding upstream and RRM1 binding downstream) in a context where both RRMs interact intramolecularly as depicted in Figure 4E,F.
evidence: This is inference from combining structural and functional data.

claim: The optimal recognition motif for RRM1 and RRM2 was determined as 5´-U/CAGG-3´ and 5´-U/CAGN-3´, respectively.
source: In this work, we could determine the optimal recognition motif for RRM1 and RRM2 as 5´-U/CAGG-3´ and 5´-U/CAGN-3´, respectively.
evidence: This is inference from structural and ITC data.

claim: The consensus motif of 5´-YAG-3´ found by Jain and co-workers using HTS-EQ on the HIV ESS3 hnRNP A1 binding site also favored a G immediately 3´ to the motif.
source: The same preference was found by Jain and co-workers using HTS-EQ on the HIV ESS3 hnRNP A1 binding site (Jain et al., 2017). Their consensus motif of 5´-YAG-3´ also favored a G immediately 3´ to the motif.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The preference for 5´-UAG-3´ can explain the increased predilection of hnRNP A1 for SMN2 exon 7 caused by the C-to-U mutation at position 6.
source: This can explain the increased predilection of hnRNP A1 for SMN2 exon 7 caused by the C-to-U mutation at position 6 (Kashima and Manley, 2003).
evidence: This is inference from the determined binding preferences and citation to a previous study.

claim: A dimerization of hnRNP A1 RRMs was proposed for binding longer RNA stretches and/or to distant RNA-binding motifs on pre-mRNAs based on the crystal structure of UP1 bound to telomeric DNA repeats.
source: On the basis of the crystal structure of UP1 bound to telomeric DNA repeats, a dimerization of hnRNP A1 RRMs was proposed for binding longer RNA stretches and/or to distant RNA-binding motifs on pre-mRNAs such as alternative 5´-splice sites (Ding et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: HnRNP A1 RRMs can bind to RNA containing two AG-binding sites without dimerization.
source: We could show here that hnRNP A1 RRMs can bind to RNA containing two AG-binding sites without dimerization.
evidence: This is supported by NMR and PRE data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The simultaneous binding of the same RNA by the tandem RRMs loops out the linker RNA sequence.
source: This simultaneous binding of the same RNA by the tandem RRMs loops out the linker RNA sequence (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is supported by the structural model shown in Figure 4.

claim: HnRNP A1 binds ISS-N1 with a directionality, RRM2 contacting the 5´ motif and RRM1 the 3´ one.
source: In addition, we show that hnRNP A1 binds ISS-N1 with a directionality, RRM2 contacting the 5´ motif and RRM1 the 3´ one.
evidence: This is supported by NMR and PRE data.

claim: The mode of binding determined with the UP1-R140A mutant is preserved with the wild-type protein, as revealed by the spin-label experiments.
source: In the case of the RNA mutant ISS-N1-u25g, the mode of binding determined with the protein mutant is preserved with the wild-type protein, as revealed by the spin-label experiments (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by PRE data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The mode of binding determined for ISS-N1 is rather insensitive to variations in the RNA sequence that is recognized.
source: In addition, as far as we could judge from our NMR titrations (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Appendix 2), the mode of binding determined here is rather insensitive to variations in the RNA sequence that is recognized.
evidence: This is inference from NMR titration data.

claim: Directionality of binding is probably driven by additional contacts from the protein towards the linker RNA.
source: This indicates that directionality is probably driven by additional contacts from the protein towards the linker RNA.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that binding topology is insensitive to sequence variations.

claim: Any binding motifs separated by spacers of a similar length as ISS-N1's down to four nucleotides could potentially be accommodated in the same manner based on the structural model and splicing assays.
source: Any binding motifs separated by spacers of a similar length as ISS-N1's down to four nucleotides could potentially be accommodated in the same manner based on our structural model and our splicing assays (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: This is inference from structural modeling and functional data.

claim: A shorter spacer than four nucleotides would prevent the simultaneous binding of both RRMs.
source: While a shorter spacer would prevent the simultaneous binding of both RRMs, a different situation has to be considered for very long spacers.
evidence: This is inference from structural constraints.

claim: It is perfectly conceivable that hnRNP A1 RRMs could bind to RNA-motifs with very long spacers simultaneously, but the directionality observed here would not be the only one occurring in such situations.
source: It is perfectly conceivable that hnRNP A1 RRMs could bind to such RNA-motifs simultaneously, but it is rather unlikely that the directionality observed here would be the only one occurring in such situations.
evidence: This is speculation about binding to RNAs with very long spacers.

claim: The study explains why the FDA approved drug SPINRAZA is so efficient in blocking A1 recruitment on ISS-N1 as it targets both RRM binding sites.
source: This new information can be very helpful to design new ASO therapeutic oligos preventing hnRNP A1 binding to pre-mRNA such as the one developed against SMA (SPINRAZA (Nusinersen)). Our study explains why this FDA approved drug is so efficient in blocking A1 recruitment on ISS-N1 as it targets both RRM binding sites.
evidence: This is inference from the structural and functional data about the binding mode.

claim: The mode of binding determined for ISS-N1 is likely to be found in many regulatory binding sites of hnRNP A1 in natural pre-mRNAs.
source: However, in the case of RNA stretches from natural pre-mRNAs, the mode of binding determined here for ISS-N1 is likely to be found in many regulatory binding sites of hnRNP A1.
evidence: This is speculation based on the flexibility of spacer length.

claim: It is highly probable to find two binding motifs next to each other in pre-mRNAs, if one does not shorten the length of the spacer too much.
source: As a matter of fact, since individual RNA-binding motifs for single RRMs are short (from 3 to 4 nucleotides), it is highly probable to find two binding motifs next to each other, if one does not shorten the length of the spacer too much.
evidence: This is inference based on the short length of individual binding motifs.

claim: The close interaction between RRM1 and RRM2 of hnRNP A1 governs how RNA is bound and recognized by the individual RRMs.
source: The close interaction between RRM1 and RRM2 of hnRNP A1 governs how RNA is bound and recognized by the individual RRMs.
evidence: This is inference from structural and binding data.

claim: High affinity binding of RRM1 can only be reached by supplementing RRM1 with the IRL.
source: High affinity binding of RRM1, can only be reached by supplementing RRM1 with the IRL.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data comparing isolated RRM1 to RRM1 in the context of UP1.

claim: The importance of the interplay between RRM1 and the IRL is reflected by the strong evolutionary conservation of both RRM1 and the IRL.
source: The importance of this interplay is reflected by the strong evolutionary conservation of both RRM1 and the IRL (Mayeda et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The additional contacts provided by the IRL help increasing the RNA-binding affinity of RRM1 by several orders of magnitude.
source: The additional contacts provided by the IRL (Ding et al., 1999; Morgan et al., 2015) help increasing the RNA-binding affinity of RRM1 by several orders of magnitude (Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Table 4 and citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The presence of a guanine 3´ to the AG core motif is no longer necessary to reach nanomolar affinity for RRM1 in the context of UP1.
source: Furthermore, the presence of a guanine 3´ to the AG core motif is no longer necessary to reach nanomolar affinity.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Table 4.

claim: It is the inter-RRM interaction that defines and constrains the IRL.
source: It is the inter-RRM interaction that defines and constrains the IRL.
evidence: This is inference from structural data.

claim: Disruption of the inter-RRM interface impedes hnRNP A1 function as a splicing repressor.
source: Hence, disruption of this interface impedes hnRNP A1 function as a splicing repressor (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by splicing assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Comparable observations to the disruption of hnRNP A1 inter-RRM interface have been made upon disruption of the RRM3-RRM4 interface of PTBP1.
source: Comparable observations have been made upon disruption of the RRM3-RRM4 interface of PTBP1 (Lamichhane et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The double-RRM2 hnRNP A1 construct tested by Mayeda et al. was as active as hnRNP A1, most probably because RRM2 is an independent domain and has the same RNA binding properties as within UP1 or hnRNP A1.
source: In previous experiments, out of several chimera, only the double-RRM2 hnRNP A1 construct tested by Mayeda et al. was as active as hnRNP A1, most probably because RRM2 is an independent domain and has the same RNA binding properties as within UP1 or hnRNP A1 (Table 4) (Mayeda et al., 1998).
evidence: This is inference from ITC data and citation to a previous study.

claim: It is crucial for the single RRM2 construct to contain the C-terminal helix to observe activity comparable to hnRNP A1.
source: However, to observe such a result it is crucial for the single RRM2 construct to contain the C-terminal helix.
evidence: This is inference from structural and binding data.

claim: Constructs excluding α3 in isolated RRM2 or UP1 or with mutations preventing the folding of α3 (M186A) perform similarly to RRM1 in isolation in terms of affinity decrease.
source: Constructs excluding α3 in isolated RRM2 (Levengood et al., 2012) or UP1 (Shamoo et al., 1994) or with mutations preventing the folding of α3 (M186A, Tables 2 and 3) perform similarly to RRM1 in isolation in terms of affinity decrease.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data and citations to previous studies.

claim: The example of the hnRNP A1 RRMs illustrates the importance of the context placement to decipher the biological function.
source: While for many studies it can be necessary to examine the behavior of single domains in isolation, this example of the hnRNP A1 RRMs illustrates the importance of the context placement to decipher the biological function.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the study.

claim: The ability by both RRMs to bind RNA is a prerequisite for hnRNP A1 mediated splicing repression.
source: The ability by both RRMs to bind RNA is a prerequisite for hnRNP A1 mediated splicing repression (Figure 5A,C) (Mayeda et al., 1994, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by splicing assay data and citations to previous studies.

claim: Both RRMs are crucial and necessary for strong SMN exon 7 splicing repression.
source: Our splicing experiments in cells demonstrate that both RRMs are crucial and necessary for strong SMN exon 7 splicing repression.
evidence: This is supported by splicing assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The individual mutations of the two RRMs were not equivalent in their effects on splicing.
source: However, the individual mutations of the two RRMs were not equivalent.
evidence: This is supported by splicing assay data showing different effects for R1r2 and r1R2.

claim: A dominant negative effect was observed only for the hnRNP A1 R1r2 variant in SMN2 splicing but not for the r1R2 variant.
source: We could observe a dominant negative effect only for the hnRNP A1 R1r2 variant in SMN2 splicing but not for the r1R2 variant.
evidence: This is supported by splicing assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Different binding geometries upon RRM mutation have different downstream effects, either through interaction with endogenous hnRNP A1 or other proteins bound to the RNA.
source: A conceivable explanation could be that the different binding geometries upon RRM mutation (as illustrated in Figure 6A) have different downstream effects, either through interaction with endogenous hnRNP A1 or other proteins bound to the RNA.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the dominant negative effect.

claim: Loss of a single hnRNP A1 binding site in the ISS-N1 of SMN2 is sufficient to impair exon 7 splicing suppression by hnRNP A1 to an extent where even overexpression of hnRNP A1 cannot rescue the aberrant splicing.
source: We provide now evidence that loss of a single hnRNP A1 binding site in the ISS-N1 of SMN2 is sufficient to impair exon 7 splicing suppression by hnRNP A1 to an extent where even overexpression of hnRNP A1 cannot rescue the aberrant splicing (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by splicing assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Loss of both binding sites in ISS-N1 results in even higher exon 7 inclusion than loss of a single site.
source: As anticipated, loss of both binding sites results in even higher exon 7 inclusion.
evidence: This is supported by splicing assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Similar observations to the importance of both ISS-N1 binding sites have been made by Hua and coworkers.
source: Similar observations have been made by Hua and coworkers (Hua et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Shortening the spacer length below four nucleotides between the two AG sites had a negative effect on exon 7 splicing repression.
source: Since shortening the spacer length below four nucleotides between the two AG sites had a negative effect on exon 7 splicing repression (Figure 5F)
evidence: This is supported by splicing assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: No rescue of hnRNP A1 function was observed when co-transfecting both single RRM mutants impaired in their RNA-binding capacities (R1r2 and r1R2).
source: and since no rescue of hnRNP A1 function was observed when co-transfecting both single RRM mutants impaired in their RNA-binding capacities (R1r2 and r1R2; Figure 5—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This is supported by splicing assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: ISS-N1 is most likely bound by a single hnRNP A1 protein in cells.
source: we can conclude that ISS-N1 is most likely bound by a single hnRNP A1 protein in cells.
evidence: This is inference from multiple lines of functional data.

claim: HnRNP A1 can spread cooperatively with a preference to do so in the 3´-to-5´ direction.
source: Taking into account, that hnRNP A1 can spread cooperatively with a preference to do so in the 3´-to-5´ direction (Okunola and Krainer, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: HnRNP A1 may oligomerize initially from ISS-N1 binding.
source: one could envisage from our data that hnRNP A1 may oligomerize initially from ISS-N1 binding.
evidence: This is speculation based on the binding data and known properties of hnRNP A1.

claim: The distance of the ISS-N1 in respect to exon 7 is important and moving it further downstream weakens its repressive character.
source: Accordingly, it is known that the distance of the ISS-N1 in respect to exon 7 is important and that moving it further downstream weakens its repressive character (Singh et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In a severe SMA mouse model a modified U1 snRNA targeted to bind just downstream of the ISS-N1 can rescue exon 7 splicing.
source: Moreover, in a severe SMA mouse model a modified U1 snRNA targeted to bind just downstream of the ISS-N1 can rescue exon 7 splicing (Rogalska et al., 2016) in agreement with a competition between hnRNP A1 and U1 snRNA for binding at the very start of intron 7.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Spreading in the 3´-to-5´ direction could originate from the position of RRM2 at the 5´-end of ISS-N1.
source: Spreading in the 3´-to-5´ direction could originate from the position of RRM2 at the 5´-end of ISS-N1.
evidence: This is speculation based on the determined binding topology.

claim: Oligomerization of hnRNP A1 along the SMN2 pre-mRNA is likely to be mediated not only by RRM-RNA binding but also by the G-domain which could interact with other hnRNP A1 molecules and RNA.
source: Oligomerization of hnRNP A1 along the SMN2 pre-mRNA is likely to be mediated not only by RRM-RNA binding but also by the G-domain which could interact with other hnRNP A1 molecules and RNA.
evidence: This is speculation based on known properties of the G-domain.

claim: RRM2 could be crucial to bring the G-rich tail near the RNA 5´-end to spread from there.
source: Hence RRM2 could then be crucial to bring the G-rich tail near the RNA 5´-end to spread from there (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of oligomerization.
